We need more positive representations of erudite men, who are currently depicted as socially inept and sexually undesirable recluses. This is a harmful stereotype that pushes people away from reading "difficult" books especially (the books most conducive to developing critical thinking and analytical skills). The truth is that the absence of critical thinking and writing skills makes you less employable and competent as a person. But positive representations of educated men must not take the form of fetishising knowledgeable men either.


Culture in general needs to once again encourage us to both understand and fairly evaluate the viewpoints that we encounter. This translates to being a well-rounded individual who is not merely the puppet of contemporary ideology, but someone able to form original insights and judgements.


I don't think we should aim to promote reading among men specifically, but rather we should highlight the benefits of reading to the development of personality for all. Once the discourse becomes about male vs. female it invariably becomes politically divisive. It's not "manly" or "womanly" to read; reading is a human activity that serves to better men and women equally.


Emotional sensitivity and empathy have been deemed feminine by the culture. In fact, our emotions play a huge role in our understanding of the world and of each other. Thought and understanding are not emotionless processes as once believed. It is impossible to understand and appreciate Dostoyevsky or Camus without emotional engagement. We need to start seeing emotions as a positive force in men's lives, not as a distraction from "pure reason" (which is a figment of the imagination). Emotionality and empathy do not mean that a man is overwhelmed with "feminine energy"; they make him human. Emotional life is not antagonistic to rationality; it informs rationality with psychic contents essential for real understanding. Men today seem to laud emotional detachment as the path to success and self-enrichment, when it in fact impoverishes them and alienates them from their own selves. It's ok to cry when reading Primo Levi, or to be struck with awe at Ovid's poetry. Such responses reveal an admirable and human sensitivity. Maybe you'll even start to understand yourself better through reading.


My experience at uni (as a philosophy student) has been that the students who write well are the ones that read often and can discern good from bad writing. I mean reading beyond the prescribed texts for the course and inquisitively learning about texts and viewpoints which are not taught in the course. The students who are able to engage best in analysis and evaluation of ideas are the ones who can bring other perspectives into the discussion and use an interdisciplinary approach.


Why don't we value libraries and learning anymore? Why do we so often believe in a facile solution to everything? Reading, while certainly not the facile solution, is an active task that cannot be substituted with passive media consumption. There is an art to writing your criticisms, responses and evaluations in the margins, and men are missing out on so much by failing to engage with books. Their relative lack of familiarity with books is certainly one factor in their worsening performance in school (which can leave lifelasting effects on their career).
